subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 10 periods = 450 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 7h 30min

textbook_items_in_class.description: Fold different types of paper (regular sheet, newspaper, tissue) repeatedly and record how many times each can be folded. Observe the pattern of thickness doubling with each fold.
Fill in the missing thickness values in the table for folds 18–26 (given fold 17 ≈ 131 cm, fold 20 ≈ 10.4 m) and then for folds 27–30 and 31–45 to experience the scale of exponential growth.

time_bands.activity: Students fold a regular sheet, newspaper, and tissue paper as many times as possible and record fold counts. Activity 1, p.19 ("Fold different types of paper repeatedly and record how many times....")
Class pools fold counts; teacher presents the doubling-thickness observation and asks students to articulate the pattern in their own words before any notation is introduced.
Students work through Activity 2, p.20 ("Fill in the missing thickness values in the table for folds 18–26....") in pairs, computing successive doublings and entering values into the table.

Math Talk, section 2.1 p.20 ("Fill the table of paper-fold thicknesses for folds 18–26, then 27–30, then 31–45....") — groups share surprising results (thickness exceeding 7,00,000 km at 46 folds) and name the pattern as 'multiplicative growth'.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly underestimate how quickly doubling accumulates — use their guesses from the opening fold to make the contrast vivid. Watch for errors in successive doubling where students add rather than multiply the previous value. The astonishment at fold 46 is the hook that motivates the need for compact notation in the next unit.

periods.activity_title: From Doubling Tables to Reasoning About Growth

textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill the table of paper-fold thicknesses for folds 18–26, then 27–30, then 31–45. Observe and discuss the pattern of exponential growth.

time_bands.activity: Students complete any remaining rows in Math Talk, section 2.1 p.20 ("Fill the table of paper-fold thicknesses for folds 18–26, then 27–30, then 31–45....") and check each other's values.

Teacher-led discussion: why does adding a fixed amount each time produce slow growth while multiplying by a fixed amount explodes? Students construct a parallel additive table (e.g., thickness increasing by 0.1 mm each fold) to compare side by side.
Groups reason aloud: 'Is there a shorter way to write 2 multiplied by itself 46 times?' Students record their proposed shorthand and explain the logic in their own words.

Brief whole-class share: one representative from each group writes their notation on the board; class evaluates which notation is clearest and most compact — setting the stage for formal exponential notation.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that thickness doubles with every fold, the key reasoning task here is contrasting multiplicative and additive growth explicitly — students should be able to articulate why the two tables diverge so dramatically. A common error is treating exponential growth as 'just fast addition'; press students to identify what is structurally different. Self-study pointer: re-reading the completed table in Activity 2, p.20 and predicting fold 50 strengthens the intuition before formal notation is introduced.
materials: Completed fold tables from the paper-folding activity
Blank comparison table (additive vs multiplicative, drawn by students)

periods.activity_title: Naming Powers — Notation and Prime Factorisation

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.2 p.22
textbook_items_in_class.description: Express repeated-multiplication expressions in exponential form: (i) 6×6×6×6, (ii) y×y, (iii) b×b×b×b, (iv) 5×5×7×7×7, (v) 2×2×a×a, (vi) a×a×a×c×c×c×c×d.
Express 32400 as a product of prime factors in exponential form using a factor tree: 32400 = 2⁴ × 5² × 3⁴.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.2 p.23
textbook_items_in_class.description: Express each number as a product of prime-factor powers in exponential form: (i) 648, (ii) 405, (iii) 540, (iv) 3600.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.2 p.23
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write the numerical value of each exponential expression: (i) 2×10³, (ii) 7²×2³, (iii) 3×4⁴, (iv) (–3)²×(–5)², (v) 3²×10⁴, (vi) (–2)⁵×(–10)⁶.

time_bands.activity: Teacher defines base-exponent notation nᵃ as compact repeated multiplication, connecting to the paper-folding doubling pattern. Students read the definition aloud and paraphrase it in their own words.

Figure it Out Q1, section 2.2 p.22 ("Express repeated-multiplication expressions in exponential form: 6×6×6×6, y×y, b×b×b×b....") — students convert each expression independently, then compare with a partner.

Teacher walks through Example, section 2.2 p.22 ("Express 32400 as a product of prime factors in exponential form using a factor tree: 32400 = 2⁴ × 5² × 3⁴...."), then students attempt Figure it Out Q2, section 2.2 p.23 ("Express each number as a product of prime-factor powers: 648, 405, 540, 3600....") with factor trees.
Figure it Out Q3, section 2.2 p.23 ("Write the numerical value of each exponential expression: 2×10³, 7²×2³, 3×4⁴....") — students evaluate each expression and discuss sign rules for negative bases.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse nᵃ with n × a — emphasise that the exponent counts how many times the base is used as a factor, not added. For negative bases, watch for errors with even vs odd exponents and sign; (–3)² = 9 not –9 is a persistent trap. Self-study pointer: Example, section 2.2 p.22 is worth re-reading as a factor-tree model before attempting prime factorisation independently.

periods.activity_title: Laws of Exponents — Discovering and Applying Three Rules

textbook_items_in_class.description: Write p⁴ × p⁶ in exponential form: p⁴ × p⁶ = p¹⁰, illustrating the product rule nᵃ × nᵇ = nᵃ⁺ᵇ with an algebraic base.
Use the product rule to compute: (i) 2⁹, (ii) 5⁷, (iii) 4⁶ — each by splitting the exponent into two convenient parts and multiplying the resulting values.
Evaluate 4⁶ in two ways: as (4³)² = 64² = 4096 and as (4²)³ = 16³ = 4096, demonstrating the power-of-a-power rule.
Express each power as a power-of-a-power in at least two different ways: (i) 8⁶, (ii) 7¹⁵, (iii) 9¹⁴, (iv) 5⁸.
Compute 2⁵ × 5⁵ using the rule mᵃ × nᵃ = (mn)ᵃ: 2⁵ × 5⁵ = 10⁵ = 1,00,000.
Simplify 10⁴ ÷ 5⁴ using the quotient rule mᵃ ÷ nᵃ = (m÷n)ᵃ: 10⁴ ÷ 5⁴ = 2⁴ = 16.

Think about how many password combinations are possible in different real-world contexts: (i) Indian Pincodes, (ii) mobile numbers, (iii) vehicle registration numbers. Find out how these codes are allotted/generated.

time_bands.activity: Students expand p⁴ × p⁶ as a string of p's, count the factors, and conjecture the product rule. Teacher confirms with Example, section 2.2 p.24 ("Write p⁴ × p⁶ in exponential form: p⁴ × p⁶ = p¹⁰...."), then class applies Math Talk, section 2.2 p.24 ("Use the product rule to compute: 2⁹, 5⁷, 4⁶ by splitting the exponent....").

Teacher presents Example, section 2.2 p.24 ("Evaluate 4⁶ in two ways: as (4³)² and as (4²)³, demonstrating the power-of-a-power rule...."); students then tackle Figure it Out, section 2.2 p.24 ("Express each power as a power-of-a-power in at least two different ways: 8⁶, 7¹⁵, 9¹⁴, 5⁸....").

Teacher works through Example, section 2.2 p.25 ("Compute 2⁵ × 5⁵ using the rule mᵃ × nᵃ = (mn)ᵃ....") and Example, section 2.2 p.25 ("Simplify 10⁴ ÷ 5⁴ using the quotient rule mᵃ ÷ nᵃ = (m÷n)ᵃ...."); students verify both results numerically.

Try This, section 2.2 p.26 ("Think about how many password combinations are possible: Indian Pincodes, mobile numbers, vehicle registration numbers....") — students compute each count using exponential notation and discuss the combinatorics connection.

periods.teacher_notes: The three laws surface in succession; students often conflate the product rule (same base, add exponents) with the product-of-same-powers rule (same exponent, multiply bases) — drill the distinction with a pair of contrasting examples at the board. When students apply the power-of-a-power rule, watch for multiplication errors in the exponent product rather than addition. The password counting context in Try This, section 2.2 p.26 is a natural payoff; let students articulate why 10⁶ counts all 6-digit codes.

periods.activity_title: Zero and Negative Exponents — Reasoning from the Division Law

textbook_items_in_class.description: Derive the division law nᵃ ÷ nᵇ = nᵃ⁻ᵇ by cancelling common factors: 2⁴ ÷ 2³ = 2¹, 2⁴ ÷ 2² = 2², step by step.
Express 2¹⁰⁰ ÷ 2²⁵ as a power of 2 using the division rule.
Define n⁰ = 1 by applying the division rule to 2⁴ ÷ 2⁴ = 2⁰ = 1, then extend to show x⁰ = 1 for any non-zero x.
Discuss why n cannot be 0 in the division law nᵃ ÷ nᵇ = nᵃ⁻ᵇ, and define n⁰ using the derived identity 2⁴ ÷ 2⁴ = 1.
Define negative exponents: 2⁴ ÷ 2⁵ = 2⁻¹ = 1/2; 2⁴ ÷ 2¹⁰ = 2⁻⁶ = 1/64. Show that n⁻ᵃ = 1/nᵃ and equivalently nᵃ = 1/n⁻ᵃ.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents Example, section 2.3 p.27 ("Derive the division law nᵃ ÷ nᵇ = nᵃ⁻ᵇ by cancelling common factors: 2⁴ ÷ 2³ = 2¹....") step by step, then students apply Math Talk, section 2.3 p.27 ("Express 2¹⁰⁰ ÷ 2²⁵ as a power of 2 using the division rule....").

Teacher uses Example, section 2.3 p.28 ("Define n⁰ = 1 by applying the division rule to 2⁴ ÷ 2⁴ = 2⁰ = 1....") to show the logical inevitability of n⁰ = 1. Students then argue through Math Talk, section 2.3 p.28 ("Discuss why n cannot be 0 in the division law; define n⁰ using the derived identity....") in pairs and report their reasoning.

Teacher works through Example, section 2.3 p.28 ("Define negative exponents: 2⁴ ÷ 2⁵ = 2⁻¹ = 1/2; 2⁴ ÷ 2¹⁰ = 2⁻⁶ = 1/64...."), establishing n⁻ᵃ = 1/nᵃ. Students verify by multiplying nᵃ × n⁻ᵃ and confirming the result is n⁰ = 1.
Quick oral round: teacher names a power such as 5⁻³ and students state the reciprocal form; class checks whether the exponent laws still hold when one exponent is negative.

periods.teacher_notes: The critical reasoning chain runs from the division law → n⁰ = 1 → n⁻ᵃ = 1/nᵃ; students must see each step as forced by consistency, not as a new rule introduced arbitrarily. A frequent error is claiming 0⁰ = 1 — use Math Talk, section 2.3 p.28 to make explicit why the base cannot be zero. Self-study pointer: Example, section 2.3 p.28 on negative exponents is worth re-reading alongside Figure it Out, section 2.3 p.29 for additional conversion practice.

periods.activity_title: Power Lines and Integer Exponent Practice

textbook_items_in_class.description: Write equivalent forms of negative exponents: (i) 2⁻⁴, (ii) 10⁻⁵, (iii) (–7)⁻², (iv) (–5)⁻³, (v) 10⁻¹⁰⁰.
Simplify and write in exponential form: (i) 2⁻⁴ × 2⁷, (ii) 3² × 3⁻⁵ × 3⁶, (iii) p³ × p⁻¹⁰, (iv) 2⁴ × (–4)⁻², (v) 8ᵖ × 8ᵍ.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out, section 2.3 p.29 ("Write equivalent forms of negative exponents: 2⁻⁴, 10⁻⁵, (–7)⁻², (–5)⁻³, 10⁻¹⁰⁰....") — students convert each to fraction form and back, identifying sign patterns for negative bases.

Figure it Out, section 2.3 p.29 ("Simplify and write in exponential form: 2⁻⁴ × 2⁷, 3² × 3⁻⁵ × 3⁶, p³ × p⁻¹⁰....") — students apply the product rule and division rule with integer (including negative) exponents, working independently then checking in pairs.

Figure it Out, section 2.3 p.30 ("Use the power line for 7 to answer: 2401×49, 49³, 343×2401, 16807/49....") — students draw the power line for 7 from 7⁻³ to 7⁶, locate all given values, and read off products and quotients by moving up or down the line.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established n⁻ᵃ = 1/nᵃ through the division-law chain, this unit focuses on fluent application across a range of expressions. The power-line tool is powerful precisely because it makes multiplication (step up) and division (step down) visible; insist that students annotate their lines with both the power notation and the numerical value. A common slip in Figure it Out, section 2.3 p.29 is incorrect handling of (–7)⁻² — remind students that a negative base raised to an even power is positive.
materials: Ruler and plain paper for drawing power lines

periods.activity_title: Expanded Form and Scientific Notation with Powers of 10

textbook_items_in_class.description: Write 47561 in expanded form using powers of 10: (4×10⁴) + (7×10³) + (5×10²) + (6×10¹) + (1×10⁰).
Write these numbers in expanded form using powers of 10: (i) 172, (ii) 5642, (iii) 6374.
Write 561.903 in expanded form using positive and negative powers of 10: (5×10²) + (6×10¹) + (1×10⁰) + (9×10⁻¹) + (0×10⁻²) + (3×10⁻³).
Convert 5900 to scientific notation in multiple ways, establishing that the standard form is 5.9 × 10³. Similarly convert 20800 = 2.08 × 10⁴ and 80,00,000 = 8 × 10⁶.
Express the following numbers in standard (scientific) form: (i) 59,853; (ii) 65,950; (iii) 34,30,000; (iv) 70,04,00,00,000.

time_bands.activity: Teacher works through Example, section 2.4 p.30 ("Write 47561 in expanded form using powers of 10: (4×10⁴) + (7×10³) + (5×10²)...."), linking each digit-position to a power of 10. Students then complete Figure it Out, section 2.4 p.30 ("Write 172, 5642, 6374 in expanded form using powers of 10....").

Teacher extends to decimals with Example, section 2.4 p.30 ("Write 561.903 in expanded form using positive and negative powers of 10...."), emphasising that 10⁻¹ = 0.1 connects to the negative-exponent definition already established. Students write two decimal numbers of their own choosing in expanded form.

Teacher presents Example, section 2.4 p.31 ("Convert 5900 to scientific notation; establish standard form 5.9 × 10³; similarly 20800 = 2.08 × 10⁴ and 80,00,000 = 8 × 10⁶...."), clarifying the constraint 1 ≤ coefficient < 10. Students discuss why 59 × 10² is not standard form.

Figure it Out, section 2.4 p.32 ("Express in standard scientific form: 59,853; 65,950; 34,30,000; 70,04,00,00,000....") — students practise converting and check each other's work for the coefficient constraint.

periods.teacher_notes: Place value and negative powers of 10 are the conceptual payoff of the work done on negative exponents; students who connect 10⁻¹ = 1/10 = 0.1 reliably will not struggle with the decimal expansion. The most common error in scientific notation is choosing a coefficient outside [1, 10) — for instance writing 59 × 10² instead of 5.9 × 10³; treat this not as a rule to memorise but as a uniqueness argument. Self-study pointer: Example, section 2.4 p.31 on multiple representations of 5900 is an excellent reference for this uniqueness idea.
materials: Place-value chart (drawn by teacher on board)

periods.activity_title: Estimation and Scientific Notation in Real Contexts

textbook_items_in_class.description: Model the Tulābhāra problem: assuming Roxie's weight = 45 kg and jaggery cost = ₹70/kg, compute worth of donated jaggery = 45 × 70 = ₹3150; similarly for wheat.
Estimate the worth (in rupees) of jaggery equal to Roxie's weight and wheat equal to Estu's weight for the Tulābhāra scenario. Make necessary assumptions about weights and current market prices.
Estimate the number of 1-rupee coins needed to equal a person's weight. First guess instinctively, then model and compute. Extend to 5-rupee coins and 10-rupee notes.
Calculate the number of 20 cm steps in a ladder to the Moon (3,84,400 km), deriving 1,92,20,00,000 steps ≈ 1.922 × 10⁹ — linear growth — contrasted with just 46 exponential folds.

Calculate using scientific notation from the animal-population data: (i) ants per human, (ii) number of starling flocks of 10,000, (iii) total leaves if each of 3×10¹² trees has 10⁴ leaves, (iv) sheets of paper needed to reach the Moon.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents Example, section 2.5 p.33 ("Model the Tulābhāra problem: Roxie's weight 45 kg, jaggery ₹70/kg, donated jaggery worth ₹3150...."), emphasising the two-phase approach: instinctive guess first, then systematic computation. Students then tackle Figure it Out, section 2.5 p.33 ("Estimate worth of jaggery equal to Roxie's weight and wheat equal to Estu's weight; make assumptions about prices....").

Try This, section 2.5 p.34 ("Estimate the number of 1-rupee coins to equal a person's weight; guess first, then compute; extend to 5-rupee coins and 10-rupee notes....") — students state guesses before computing, then express answers in scientific notation.

Teacher walks through Example, section 2.5 p.35 ("Calculate the number of 20 cm steps in a ladder to the Moon: 1,92,20,00,000 steps ≈ 1.922 × 10⁹ — contrasted with 46 exponential folds...."), making the additive-vs-multiplicative contrast vivid with a side-by-side comparison.

Figure it Out, section 2.5 p.38 ("Calculate using scientific notation: ants per human, starling flocks, total leaves on 3×10¹² trees, sheets of paper to the Moon....") — students compute each in pairs, expressing results in scientific notation and ordering the quantities by magnitude.

periods.teacher_notes: The two-phase approach (guess then compute) is central to this unit — resist skipping the guess phase, because the gap between intuition and result is the pedagogical point. Students often forget to express final answers in scientific notation after arithmetic; build this as a habitual last step. Watch for unit-conversion errors when students move between km, m, and cm in the Moon-ladder problem.
materials: Pencil and paper for estimation work

textbook_items_in_class.description: Estimate Roxie's age in hours (given she completed 13 years a few weeks ago), and find Estu's date of birth given he is 4070 days old. Find out how old you would be if you had lived for a million seconds.

Calculate using scientific notation from the time-scale data: (i) time in seconds to count all stars in the universe (2×10²³) at one per second; (ii) time to drink all water on Earth (200 ml/glass every 10 seconds).
Think of real-world events or phenomena whose duration is of the order of (i) 10⁵ seconds and (ii) 10⁶ seconds. Write them in scientific notation.
Estimate how many people might benefit from donating notebooks equal to one's weight annually, and from annadāna equal to one's weight. Guess first, then compute.

time_bands.activity: Try This, section 2.5 p.39 ("Estimate Roxie's age in hours; find Estu's date of birth from 4070 days; find your age if you had lived a million seconds....") — students convert years to hours, days to calendar dates, and seconds to years, expressing each in scientific notation.

Figure it Out, section 2.5 p.42 ("Calculate time in seconds to count 2×10²³ stars at one per second; time to drink all Earth's water at 200 ml every 10 seconds....") — students set up the division and multiplication, express results in scientific notation, and compare to the geological timescale in the section.

Try This, section 2.5 p.42 ("Think of real-world events whose duration is of the order of 10⁵ seconds and 10⁶ seconds....") — students brainstorm in small groups, compare suggestions, and write each duration in scientific notation.

Math Talk, section 2.5 p.34 ("Estimate how many people might benefit from donating notebooks equal to one's weight; guess first, then compute....") — class discusses, connects to the Tulābhāra context, and interprets results using powers of 10.

periods.teacher_notes: The time-scale problems invite students to appreciate that powers of 10 carry meaning about the order of magnitude of real phenomena — a conceptual step beyond mere computation. Watch for errors in unit conversion between seconds, minutes, hours, and years; insist students write conversion chains explicitly. Linking the geological timeline in the section to Try This, section 2.5 p.42 gives students a concrete feel for what 10⁵ vs 10⁶ seconds looks like in lived experience.
materials: Timeline chart (drawn on board by teacher)

periods.activity_title: Indian Traditions of Large Numbers and Exponential Puzzles

textbook_items_in_class.description: What does the first part of each name (million, billion, trillion, quadrillion …) denote in the American naming system?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.5A p.44
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the units digit in the value of 22²⁴ ÷ 43². [Hint: 4 = 2²]

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.5A p.44
textbook_items_in_class.description: There are 5 bottles in a container. Every day a new container is brought in. How many bottles are there after 40 days?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.5A p.44
textbook_items_in_class.description: Examine each statement and decide if it is Always True, Only Sometimes True, or Never True: (i) cube numbers are also square numbers; (ii) fourth powers are also square numbers; (iii) fifth power divisible by cube; (iv) product of two cubes is a cube; (v) q⁴⁶ is both a 4th power and a 6th power.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 2.5A p.45
textbook_items_in_class.description: The worldwide population of sheep and goats is each about 10⁹. What is the total population? Choose the correct option from: (i) 20⁹, (ii) 10¹¹, (iii) 10¹⁰, (iv) 10¹⁸, (v) 2×10⁹, (vi) 10⁹+10⁹.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q13, section 2.5A p.45
textbook_items_in_class.description: Calculate and write in scientific notation: (i) total pieces of clothing if each of 8.2×10⁹ people has 30 pieces; (ii) total honeybees if 10⁸ colonies each have 50,000 bees; (iii) total bacterial cells in all humans (38 trillion per person × world population); (iv) total time spent eating in a lifetime in seconds.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the Indian naming tradition for large powers of 10 (lakh, crore, arab, kharab through to names from Lalitavistara and Mahaviracharya's Ganita-sara-sangraha) and the American system (million, billion, trillion). Students work through Figure it Out, section 2.5A p.43 ("What does the first part of each name — million, billion, trillion, quadrillion — denote in the American system?...") and map each name to its power of 10.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q1, section 2.5A p.44 ("Find the units digit in the value of 22²⁴ ÷ 43²....") using the hint 4 = 2², and Figure it Out Q2, section 2.5A p.44 ("There are 5 bottles in a container; every day a new container is brought in; how many bottles after 40 days?...") by identifying the exponential model.

Figure it Out Q4, section 2.5A p.44 ("Examine each statement — Always True, Only Sometimes True, or Never True: cube numbers are also squares; fourth powers are also squares; fifth powers divisible by cubes....") — students reason in pairs, justify with examples or counter-examples, and report to the class.

Figure it Out Q12, section 2.5A p.45 ("Sheep and goats each about 10⁹; which option gives the total?...") — class reasons through the options to see why 2×10⁹ is correct but 20⁹ is not. Then Figure it Out Q13, section 2.5A p.45 ("Calculate total clothing, honeybees, bacterial cells, eating-time in scientific notation....") — students compute two of the four parts in pairs.

periods.teacher_notes: The historical thread — Indian naming systems for powers up to 10⁹⁶ and beyond — connects the chapter's notation to a living cultural tradition; encourage students to identify whether their own home languages have names for large numbers. A persistent error in Q12 is choosing 10¹⁰ (treating 10⁹ + 10⁹ as 10¹⁸); make explicit that addition of equal powers multiplies the coefficient by 2, not the exponent. Figure it Out Q4 develops the Always/Sometimes/Never reasoning that the adjunct competency strand requires and rewards precise thinking about what makes a statement universally vs conditionally true.
materials: Reference list of Indian large-number names (written on board by teacher)

items.prompt: A sheet of paper is 0.1 mm thick. Each time it is folded, its thickness doubles. What is the thickness of the paper after 4 folds?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1.6 mm. Starting thickness = 0.1 mm; after 4 folds the thickness is 0.1 × 2⁴ = 0.1 × 16 = 1.6 mm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the starting thickness by 2 raised to the number of folds: thickness = 0.1 × 2⁴.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student multiplied 0.1 by 4 (additive thinking) rather than by 2⁴ (multiplicative thinking).
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student computed 0.1 × 2³ = 0.8, applying one too few doublings — likely counted folds from 0 incorrectly.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student computed 0.1 × 2⁵ = 3.2, applying one too many doublings — an off-by-one error in the fold count.

inclusivity.support: Let the student draw a table starting at 0.1 mm and double the value row by row for four rows.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state the thickness after n folds as a general expression and explain why it grows so much faster than adding 0.1 mm each time.

exercise.description: Fold different types of paper (regular sheet, newspaper, tissue) repeatedly and record how many times each can be folded. Observe the pattern of thickness doubling with each fold.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly expresses 3 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 5 in exponential form?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3³ × 5². There are three factors of 3 and two factors of 5, giving 3³ × 5².
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count how many times each base appears as a factor and write that count as the exponent.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student counted the total number of factors (5) and assigned it as the exponent of 3, ignoring the two different bases.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student multiplied the bases (3 × 5 = 15) and used the total factor count as the exponent — conflating product-of-same-powers with base counting.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student swapped the exponents, writing 3² × 5³ — likely confused which base appears more often.

inclusivity.support: Let the student write out the product long-hand and circle all 3s and all 5s separately before writing the exponential form.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write a×a×a×c×c×c×c×d in exponential form and explain the role of each base and its exponent.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.2 p.22
exercise.description: Express repeated-multiplication expressions in exponential form: (i) 6×6×6×6, (ii) y×y, (iii) b×b×b×b, (iv) 5×5×7×7×7, (v) 2×2×a×a, (vi) a×a×a×c×c×c×c×d.

items.prompt: In the American naming system for large numbers, the name 'billion' represents which power of 10?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 10⁹. In the American system each new name (million, billion, trillion) is 1000 times the previous: million = 10⁶, billion = 10⁹.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The American system advances by a factor of 1000 (10³) at each new name: 10⁶ → 10⁹ → 10¹².

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student identified million (10⁶) rather than billion — confused the first large-number name with the second.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be thinking of ten million (10⁷), confusing the Indian system's crore (10⁷) with the American billion.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be thinking of 10⁸ as a midpoint between million and billion, without recognising the 10³ step.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the Indian and American naming comparison in section 2.5A and fill in a two-column table: Name | Power of 10.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state what power of 10 'quadrillion' represents and to explain the pattern in one sentence using the phrase 'factor of 1000'.

exercise.description: What does the first part of each name (million, billion, trillion, quadrillion …) denote in the American naming system?

items.prompt: A student claims: 'If I add 10 to a number 46 times, I will get as large a result as multiplying the number by 2 forty-six times.' Is this claim correct? Explain your reasoning using the paper-folding context.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The claim is incorrect. Repeated addition of 10 gives a total increase of 46 × 10 = 460 (linear growth), whereas starting with, say, 0.1 mm and doubling 46 times gives 0.1 × 2⁴⁶ ≈ 7,000,000,000 mm — roughly 7,000 km — an incomparably larger result. Multiplicative (exponential) growth increases by a fixed ratio each step, so the output grows without bound far faster than additive growth.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the additive total (46 × fixed amount) with the multiplicative result (starting value × 2⁴⁶) to show exponential growth vastly outpaces linear growth.

inclusivity.support: Invite the student to complete two short rows — one additive, one multiplicative — starting from 1 for the first five steps, and describe aloud what they notice.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what if the multiplier were 1.5 instead of 2? Would the gap between additive and multiplicative growth still grow without bound? Justify your answer.

exercise.description: Fill the table of paper-fold thicknesses for folds 18–26, then 27–30, then 31–45. Observe and discuss the pattern of exponential growth.

items.prompt: Using only the division rule nᵃ ÷ nᵇ = nᵃ⁻ᵇ and what you know about dividing a number by itself, explain step by step why any non-zero number raised to the power zero must equal 1. Then explain why we require n ≠ 0 for this to make sense.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1: Choose any non-zero base, say n = 5, and the same exponent on top and bottom: 5³ ÷ 5³. Step 2: Any non-zero number divided by itself equals 1, so 5³ ÷ 5³ = 1. Step 3: Applying the division rule: 5³ ÷ 5³ = 5³⁻³ = 5⁰. Step 4: Therefore 5⁰ = 1. The same argument works for any non-zero base n, giving n⁰ = 1. If n = 0, step 2 fails because 0 ÷ 0 is undefined — we cannot divide by zero — so the argument breaks down and 0⁰ is left undefined.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the division rule to nᵃ ÷ nᵃ = nᵃ⁻ᵃ = n⁰, then observe independently that nᵃ ÷ nᵃ = 1 for any non-zero n.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to first compute 2³ ÷ 2³ numerically (getting 1) and then apply the division rule to the same expression; let them see that the two results must be equal.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: does the same reasoning force the value of (–3)⁰? What if the base is a fraction like (2/5)⁰? Extend the argument.

exercise.description: Express 2¹⁰⁰ ÷ 2²⁵ as a power of 2 using the division rule.

items.prompt: A 3-digit lock uses the digits 0–9 on each dial. A 4-letter lock uses the letters A–Z on each dial. Without using a calculator, find (i) the number of codes possible on the 3-digit lock, and (ii) the number of codes possible on the 4-letter lock. Express both answers in exponential form and then evaluate (i) numerically.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (i) Each of the 3 dials has 10 choices, giving 10 × 10 × 10 = 10³ = 1000 codes. (ii) Each of the 4 dials has 26 choices, giving 26 × 26 × 26 × 26 = 26⁴ codes (= 4,56,976, though the numerical value is not required).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the counting principle: when each position has k independent choices, n positions give kⁿ total codes.

inclusivity.support: Draw a tree diagram for a 2-digit lock with only 3 digits (0,1,2) to see 3² = 9 branches, then scale up the reasoning.
inclusivity.challenge: A lock has 3 dials: the first uses digits 0–9, the second uses letters A–Z, and the third uses digits 0–9. How many codes are possible? Express the answer using the product-of-powers idea.

exercise.description: Use the product rule to compute: (i) 2⁹, (ii) 5⁷, (iii) 4⁶ — each by splitting the exponent into two convenient parts and multiplying the resulting values.

items.prompt: Simplify the following expression and write the result as a single power: 3⁵ × 3⁻² ÷ 3³. Then write the numerical value of your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3⁵ × 3⁻² ÷ 3³ = 3⁽⁵⁺⁽⁻²⁾⁻³⁾ = 3⁰ = 1. Alternate check: 3⁵ = 243, 3⁻² = 1/9, 3³ = 27; then 243 × (1/9) ÷ 27 = 27 ÷ 27 = 1. Both routes confirm the answer is 1.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the product rule (add exponents for multiplication) and division rule (subtract exponent for division), all with the same base 3.

inclusivity.support: Let the student first convert 3⁻² to 1/9, compute 3⁵ × (1/9) ÷ 3³ numerically step by step, and then match to the exponent-rule route.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the expression to 3⁵ × 3⁻ᵏ ÷ 3³ and find the value of k that makes the result equal to 9. Justify your answer.

exercise.description: Write equivalent forms of negative exponents: (i) 2⁻⁴, (ii) 10⁻⁵, (iii) (–7)⁻², (iv) (–5)⁻³, (v) 10⁻¹⁰⁰.

items.prompt: Write the number 3,04,050 in (i) expanded form using powers of 10, and (ii) standard scientific notation (x × 10ʸ where 1 ≤ x < 10).

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write each digit multiplied by the power of 10 matching its place value; then move the decimal point to produce a coefficient between 1 and 10 and record the corresponding power of 10.

inclusivity.support: Give the student a place-value chart with columns labelled 10⁵ through 10⁰ and ask them to fill in each digit before writing the expanded form.
inclusivity.challenge: Now write 3,04,050.27 in expanded form using both positive and negative powers of 10, and express it in scientific notation.

exercise.description: Write these numbers in expanded form using powers of 10: (i) 172, (ii) 5642, (iii) 6374.

items.prompt: A forest has 4 × 10⁸ trees. Each tree has an average of 2 × 10⁵ leaves. Calculate the total number of leaves in the forest and express your answer in scientific notation.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the coefficients and add the exponents of 10, then verify the coefficient lies in [1, 10).

inclusivity.support: Let the student first multiply 4 × 2 = 8, then separately apply the product rule 10⁸ × 10⁵ = 10¹³, and finally combine the two results.
inclusivity.challenge: The forest is one of 6 × 10³ such forests in the country. Find the total leaf count for the country and express it in scientific notation, explaining each step.

exercise.description: Calculate using scientific notation from the animal-population data: (i) ants per human, (ii) number of starling flocks of 10,000, (iii) total leaves if each of 3×10¹² trees has 10⁴ leaves, (iv) sheets of paper needed to reach the Moon.

items.prompt: A student has been alive for exactly 11 years. Assuming each year has 365 days, calculate the student's age in (i) days, (ii) hours, and (iii) seconds. Express each answer in scientific notation.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of years by successive conversion factors (365, 24, 3600) and express each result in standard scientific notation.

inclusivity.support: Give the student the conversion chain 1 year = 365 days, 1 day = 24 hours, 1 hour = 3600 seconds as a printed chain and ask them to multiply step by step.
inclusivity.challenge: Express the student's age in seconds as a power of 10 to the nearest integer and discuss what geological or cosmological event in the chapter's timeline is closest to that duration.

exercise.description: Estimate Roxie's age in hours (given she completed 13 years a few weeks ago), and find Estu's date of birth given he is 4070 days old. Find out how old you would be if you had lived for a million seconds.
